h1: Rice varieties for rice lager in India
title: Rice Varieties for Rice Lager in India | Craft Beer School
desc: Which Indian rice suits a rice lager: brokens versus whole grain, amylose and gelatinisation, the specs to check and what basmati really adds.
teaser: Broken rice is not a compromise. For a crisp rice lager it is often the smartest buy in the market.
standfirst: India grows more rice varieties than any brewer needs. Most of them will make good beer. What matters is starch, freshness and how you cook it. We explain what to look for when buying rice for a lager.
sections: What rice does in a lager

Rice is almost pure starch with little protein, fat or flavour. In a lager grist it adds fermentable extract while thinning out the malt character. The result is a paler, crisper, drier beer with less body and a cleaner finish. That suits Indian food and Indian heat well, which is why so many mainstream Asian lagers use it.

Because rice carries no enzymes of its own, the barley malt in the grist must convert its starch. Rice also brings very little free amino nitrogen (FAN), the nitrogen yeast needs to grow. Push rice too high and the yeast runs short. Our guide to rice and maize adjuncts in India gives the wider picture.
Brokens are what most brewers buy

Rice mills produce broken grains as a by-product of polishing. Brokens have the same starch as whole grains at a much lower price, because they cannot be sold as table rice. For brewing, grain shape does not matter: the rice is going to be milled or cooked into a porridge anyway.

What does matter in brokens is cleanliness. Look for:

  • Little bran or husk. Rice bran is oily and can bring stale, rancid flavours and hurt foam.
  • No musty smell, insects or visible mould.
  • Moisture below about 14%, so it stores without spoiling.
  • A consistent supplier, so lot to lot starch content stays steady.

Rice starch is a mix of amylose and amylopectin. Most Indian table rice is indica, relatively high in amylose. Sticky or glutinous rice is almost all amylopectin. The ratio affects how the grain swells and how hot it must get before the starch gelatinises and becomes available to enzymes.

Rice gelatinises at a higher temperature than barley malt starch, commonly quoted in the range of about 68 to 78 °C, varying by variety. Barley malt starch converts at ordinary mash temperatures. That gap is why rice is usually cooked separately in a cereal cooker and brought to the boil before it joins the main mash. Our guide to starch gelatinisation temperatures explains the numbers.
Common varieties and what to expect

South Indian brewers often find Sona Masuri or Ponni brokens easily. IR64 and similar high yielding varieties are widely grown across the country. All of these make perfectly good brewing rice once cooked properly. Differences between them in the finished beer are small next to differences in freshness, bran content and process.

Basmati is the variety people ask about most. Its famous aroma comes from a volatile compound, 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline. Very little of that is likely to survive cooking, mashing, a vigorous boil and fermentation. Paying basmati prices for brewing rice buys you almost nothing in the glass. Use it only if a marketing story depends on it and you have checked the claim with your own sensory panel.
Running a small trial before you switch

Before changing rice supplier or variety in production, run a small trial. Cook a kilo of the new rice on the stove with a handful of crushed malt, holding it near 72 °C, then boiling it for 20 minutes. Watch how fast it thickens and how easily it thins once the malt enzymes act. A rice that sets like cement in the pot will do the same in your cereal cooker.

Then mash a small test with your normal malt and check the iodine test for full conversion. If the new rice converts in the same time and gives a similar extract, the switch is safe to try at full scale.

Rice shares in commercial Asian lagers vary widely. As a working range, 20 to 35% of the grist gives a noticeably lighter, crisper beer while all-malt wort still supplies enough enzymes and FAN. Above that, check FAN in the wort and consider a yeast nutrient. Our guide to low FAN worts from high rice grists covers the fix.

A worked example for a 1,000 litre rice lager at about 11 °P: 130 kg Pilsner malt (72%) and 50 kg broken rice (28%). Cook the rice with about 10% of the malt in the cereal cooker, rest briefly near 72 °C, boil for 20 to 30 minutes, then pump it into the main mash to lift it to saccharification temperature.

Rice keeps better than malt, but monsoon humidity still gets at it. Store sacks off the floor on pallets, away from walls, in a dry room. Buy in quantities you will use within a couple of months. Old rice can pick up stale, cardboard notes and attract insects. Run a simple check on each delivery: smell, look and a moisture reading if you have a meter.

Getting a high adjunct lager right means balancing starch conversion, FAN, attenuation and flavour. That is mash chemistry. It rewards brewers who understand it rather than copy a schedule.

Your first step: ask your rice supplier for a sample of brokens, check it for bran, smell and moisture, then cook a small batch on the stove to see how it behaves.
faqs: Is broken rice good enough for brewing?
Yes. Brokens have the same starch as whole grains and cost less. Check that they are clean, low in bran and dry.
Does basmati rice make a better rice lager?
Very little of basmati's aroma is likely to survive cooking, the boil and fermentation. It costs far more for little difference in the glass.
Why does rice need a cereal cooker?
Rice starch gelatinises at a higher temperature than normal mash temperatures. Boiling it separately makes the starch available to the malt's enzymes.
